props.title: Night Nurse

sections.content: **Night Nurse** (1931) exemplifies Pre-Code Hollywood's raw intensity, tackling themes later banned by the Hays Code. Barbara Stanwyck stars as Lora Hart, a nurse uncovering sinister plots against wealthy children - featuring bootlegging, child abuse, and murder. The film's unflinching approach to social issues mirrors other Pre-Code classics like **Baby Face** (1933) and **Red-Headed Woman** (1932), showing working women navigating moral grey areas. William Wellman's direction keeps tension high while exposing healthcare corruption and class exploitation. movies.title: Night Nurse
movies.slug: Barbara Stanwyck stars as a nurse who discovers a plot to murder two children in her care. Features Clark Gable as a menacing chauffeur.

sections.content: The film's depiction of healthcare corruption finds echoes in later medical dramas like **The Hospital** (1971) and **Article 99** (1992), though few match its pre-code frankness about institutional failure. Stanwyck's performance established her as one of Hollywood's most fearless actresses, building on the foundation that would lead to noir classics like **Double Indemnity** (1944). The film's mix of social commentary and thriller elements created a template for exposé films.

Clark Gable's supporting role as the villainous Nick - before his romantic leading man persona was established - showcases Pre-Code Hollywood's comfort with moral ambiguity. Like **The Public Enemy** (1931) and **Little Caesar** (1931), the film doesn't shy away from showing violence and criminal behavior, though here it's in service of exposing social ills rather than gangster glorification. sections.content: Director William Wellman's unflinching approach to medical realism influenced later hospital dramas, though few matched **Night Nurse**'s combination of procedural detail and thriller elements until **Coma** (1978). The film's frank discussion of class disparity and institutional corruption particularly resonates with later exposés like **The Snake Pit** (1948) and **One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest** (1975).
